notYet: Not yet part of the Mediterranean

stages.name: No recorded trade
stages.desc: No Levantine glass recorded in the period's evidence

stages.name: Importing Levantine glass
stages.desc: Buys glass vessels made on the Phoenician coast

stages.name: Other glass-making region
stages.desc: Makes its own glass: Alexandria, Rhodes, Italy, Gaul

stages.name: Levantine production centre
stages.desc: Phoenician coast: Belus sand, Sidon and Tyre's workshops

states.name: Cyprus
timeline: Ptolemaic Cyprus buys glass from the facing Phoenician coast
Mould-blown cups by Ennion and by Aristeas the Cypriot reach Cypriot tombs

states.name: Israel
timeline: Sand from the mouth of the Belus river near Ptolemais (Akko) feeds the region's glassmakers
A workshop in Jerusalem throws away glass tubes and small blown bottles
Herod begins the harbour city of Caesarea on the coast

states.name: Palestine
timeline: The Judaean hill country buys its glass from the coastal workshops

states.name: Lebanon
timeline: Sidon and Tyre, Phoenician cities under the Seleucid kings, cast and core-form luxury glass
Tyre wins its autonomy from the Seleucids; Sidon follows in 111 BC
Pompey annexes the coast to the new Roman province of Syria
Ennion and other Sidonian masters sign mould-blown cups

states.name: Syria
timeline: Aradus, the northern Phoenician island city, and inland Seleucid towns buy coastal glass
Becomes part of the Roman province of Syria

states.name: France
timeline: Celtic Gaul: glass bangles, but no Levantine vessels recorded; Greek Massalia on the coast
Caesar's conquest opens Gaul to Roman goods, glass among them
Glassblowing workshops open at Lugdunum (Lyon)

states.name: Turkey
timeline: Antioch, Pergamon and the cities of Asia Minor buy Hellenistic glass
Pergamon is bequeathed to Rome and becomes the province of Asia

states.name: Tunisia
timeline: Punic Carthage, Tyre's ancient colony, trades with the Phoenician East
Rome destroys Carthage; the city lies empty for a century
Augustus refounds Carthage as a Roman colony; Eastern glass returns

states.name: Greece
timeline: Rhodes runs one of the Hellenistic world's glass workshops; Delos trades in glass
Cassius sacks Rhodes; Greece now buys its glass from the East and Italy

states.name: Italy
timeline: Rome's elite buys cast and mosaic glass bowls from the Greek East
Under Augustus, Eastern glassblowers set up workshops in Rome and Campania
Glassworks spread to Aquileia and northern Italy

states.name: Egypt
timeline: Ptolemaic Alexandria makes mosaic, gold-band and cast glass; natron comes from the Wadi Natrun
Egypt becomes a Roman province; Alexandria keeps its glassworks

events.title: Sand of the Belus
events.text: The beach at the mouth of the Belus river, near Ptolemais, supplies a sand that later writers single out for glass.

events.title: Natron of Egypt
events.text: The soda for ancient glass is natron, a salt dug from the dry lakes of the Wadi Natrun and shipped from Egypt.

events.title: Rhodian glass
events.text: Workshops on Rhodes make beads and core-formed and cast vessels for the Hellenistic market.

events.title: Carthage destroyed
events.text: Rome razes Carthage, Tyre's greatest colony, ending Punic power in the west.

events.title: Corinth sacked
events.text: In the same year Rome sacks Corinth; Greece falls under Roman control.

events.title: Alexandrian luxury
events.text: Alexandria's glassmakers fuse coloured canes into mosaic bowls and sandwich gold leaf between layers of glass.

events.title: Pergamon to Rome
events.text: King Attalus III wills his kingdom to Rome, which makes it the province of Asia.

events.title: Tyre goes free
events.text: Tyre wins its autonomy from the weakening Seleucid kings; Sidon follows in 111 BC.

events.title: Glass at Tel Anafa
events.text: A rich house in Upper Galilee fills with cast drinking bowls, one of the largest Hellenistic glass finds.

events.title: Puteoli harbour
events.text: Eastern ships unload at Puteoli, Rome's great port on the Bay of Naples.

events.title: Delos sacked
events.text: Mithridates' forces sack Delos, the free port where Italian and Eastern merchants traded.

events.title: Mahdia wreck
events.text: A ship carrying Greek bronzes and marbles to Italy sinks off the African coast.

events.title: Antikythera wreck
events.text: A ship bound for Italy sinks with statues, a geared bronze mechanism and fine glass bowls.

events.title: Pompey takes Syria
events.text: Pompey ends the Seleucid kingdom and makes Syria, the Phoenician coast included, a Roman province.

events.title: Caesar in Gaul
events.text: Julius Caesar begins the conquest that brings Gaul into the Roman world.

events.title: Blown in Jerusalem
events.text: A workshop dumps glass tubes blown closed at one end and tiny bottles: the earliest closely dated blown glass.

events.title: Caesar in Alexandria
events.text: Caesar is besieged in Alexandria and sides with Cleopatra in Egypt's civil war.

events.title: Lugdunum founded
events.text: The Romans found Lugdunum, future Lyon, which becomes the capital of the Gauls.

events.title: Rhodes sacked
events.text: Cassius storms Rhodes and strips it of its wealth; the island's glory fades.

events.title: Herod's Jerusalem
events.text: Herod takes Jerusalem; under his rule the old glass dump is sealed beneath new floors.

events.title: Egypt becomes Roman
events.text: After Cleopatra's death, Egypt and Alexandria's workshops pass to Augustus.

events.title: Carthage refounded
events.text: Augustus settles Roman colonists on the ruins of Carthage.

events.title: Strabo's glassmakers
events.text: In Alexandria, the geographer Strabo hears glassworkers explain the secrets of their materials.

events.title: Caesarea begun
events.text: Herod starts building a new harbour city on the coast south of the Belus.

events.title: Blowing reaches Rome
events.text: Blown flasks and bottles appear in Rome as Eastern craftsmen settle in Italy.

events.title: Death of Augustus
events.text: Augustus dies at Nola in Campania; by now blown glass is sold across Italy.

events.title: Cup for a coin
events.text: Strabo writes that in Rome a glass cup can be bought for a small copper coin.

events.title: Ennion of Sidon
events.text: Ennion signs mould-blown cups 'Ennion made it' and asks the buyer to remember him.

events.title: Glass at Lugdunum
events.text: Glassblowers set up furnaces at Lyon, among the first in Gaul.

events.title: Aristeas the Cypriot
events.text: Another mould-blower, Aristeas the Cypriot, signs cups that reach northern Italy.

events.title: Unbreakable glass
events.text: A tale set under Tiberius has the emperor execute a man who made glass that bent but did not break.

events.title: Aquileia's furnaces
events.text: Aquileia, at the head of the Adriatic, becomes a centre of Roman glassblowing.

events.title: Ennion's cups in tombs
events.text: Cups by Ennion are buried in tombs on Cyprus and in northern Italy.

events.title: Seneca's glassblower
events.text: Seneca marvels at the craftsman who shapes glass into countless forms with his breath.

events.title: Jerusalem burns
events.text: Rome destroys Jerusalem; a burnt building holds a jug signed by Ennion.

events.title: Sand of the Volturnus
events.text: Pliny records Italian glass made from the white sand of the Volturnus, between Cumae and Liternum.

events.title: Glass in Pompeii
events.text: Pompeii's houses and shops fill with blown bottles, cups and jars; some baths have glass windows.

events.title: Pliny's Natural History
events.text: Pliny dedicates his encyclopedia, with its legend of natron merchants on the Belus beach.

events.title: Vesuvius erupts
events.text: Vesuvius buries Pompeii and Herculaneum, sealing thousands of everyday glass vessels.

events.title: Death of Pliny
events.text: Pliny, commander of the fleet at Misenum, dies at Stabiae trying to rescue people from the eruption.

eras: The blowpipe on the Levantine coast
chartNote: Share of the area of eleven present-day Mediterranean countries, by their main role in the glass trade. Most regions both made and bought glass; the map shows the leading role, and large countries such as Egypt, Turkey and France swing the shares. Regions are today's boundaries, a simplification of a world of cities, kingdoms and Roman provinces.
